title: AI in Education #2: Five Things I Learned from Barbara Oakley
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton distills five takeaways from a conversation with Barbara Oakley, distinguished professor of engineering and co-creator of the Coursera course Learning How to Learn, who did not touch maths again until age 26 after a childhood of avoiding the subject. Oakley's central argument is that automated recall does not substitute for internalised knowledge: using a hospital medication-dosage error as an analogy, she insists students need multiplication facts and number sense in their heads so they can catch an implausible answer, not just access to a calculator or AI. She frames AI's proper role as making necessary practice less tedious -- adapting difficulty and adding gamification -- rather than replacing memorisation, and argues that because AI has made homework unreliable as evidence of learning, schools should shift to frequent, low-stakes in-class retrieval quizzes done without AI access. She is enthusiastic about AI as a teacher's thought partner for generating hooks and activities but firmly against AI (or teachers) replacing carefully designed curricula, since half of all teachers are, by definition, below average. She closes by arguing that schools of education still teach outdated theorists whose approaches conflict with cognitive science, and that AI could force a reckoning by enabling teacher-training pathways built on how the brain actually learns.
points: Automated access to an answer is not the same as internalised knowledge -- a student who has memorised multiplication facts will instinctively flag 12 x 12 = 299 as wrong, while a student who has not will shrug, which is why AI or a calculator cannot substitute for practice.

AI's most defensible classroom role is making necessary-but-boring procedural practice more adaptive and engaging, not eliminating memorisation, which Oakley says 'reform methodologies' get badly wrong about how the brain works.
Because AI has made homework an unreliable signal of learning, Oakley recommends replacing it as an assessment tool with frequent, low-stakes in-class retrieval quizzes taken without AI access.

Oakley argues 'great teachers should have some freedom' with materials, but since half of all teachers are below average, tightly designed curricula (like JUMP Math) protect weaker teachers' students more than open-ended resource creation does.

Schools of education still centre theorists (Dewey, Vygotsky, Piaget, Montessori) whose prescriptions often conflict with cognitive science, and Oakley sees AI as a possible lever to build teacher-training pathways grounded in the science of learning instead.
quotes: reform methodologies that say students do not need to memorise multiplication tables because they can always look them up – those approaches know nothing about how the brain works.
Her view is blunt: if you do not see students producing answers without access to AI, you have no idea whether they know anything.
everyone loves to hate on tests, but try running schools without them. She volunteered in an inner-city school before national testing came in, and the picture she painted was grim.

Barb’s position? Great teachers should have some freedom. But the more you loosen things up, the more that weaker teachers will struggle. And as she pointed out with characteristic directness: half of all teachers are below average.
She told me she has travelled the world and heard primary teachers ask: “You mean it is okay to explain something to a student?” That is how extreme things have got in some places.
if the people training teachers do not understand the science of learning, and if they are actively promoting approaches that make learning harder, then we have a serious problem.
